editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: Today is March 6th, 2001. The interview will take place at the veteran's house. The address is 5322 South Springfield Avenue in Chicago, Illinois 60632. The name of veteran is Louis Budz. He was born on July 26th in 1915. Louis served in Army during World War II and also Korean War. My name is Manuela Capiak and I'll be conducting the interview. Okay. Louis, what was your family like, your childhood?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: Childhood days, I tell you, my family was awful, very awful. I remember the day when I was a little boy -- my mother had to struggle all her life during the Depression. My father, he hung around with Polish people and they drank, drank, drank. And I tell you one thing, I put a -- I tried to put a fire in the stove. I had nothing to eat all that day in October. And it was cold. I had no -- I just had a pair of pants, no shoes, no stocking and a shirt. I was hungry. I had nothing to eat. I put -- finally put water in the stove, killed the fire and ate that hard bread. It was hard like a rock. And he was mad, he was hollering. My sister ran away. My other sister ran away. She was young. My mother I don't know where went to. I went outside and I was -- I was scared of my father, you know. Geez, I didn't know what to do. I was eating that hard bread, cold, shaking like a leaf. The woman next door, they took me in the house. I tell you -- I was behind the stove. You had a wooden stove with coal and wood. I was like this. Like just -- God didn't want me to die. He just didn't want me. I don't know why.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: Do you remember how old were you?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: Oh, sure. 5 years old. Boy, can remember 5 -- I can even remember when the fire department used to have horses. Yeah, isn't that something? That's how far back. I can remember the guys from World War I that were fighting and they were coming through the stockyards in 1915 -- '16, I think it was. Yeah, I remember that. Oh, I can remember a lot of things. I remember when they had the Chicago fire, I used to help the firemen pull the hoses so we'd start up -- stop the fire.

So after I was there, then somehow my mother, she come home and that woman next door kept me for I don't know how long. I never forgot them. But every time they send me to go get their errands, she want to give me money. I don't know if it was a penny. A penny was a lot of money at that time. I told them, "No, you've clothed me, you've fed me, you kept me warm." I'll never forget her. Her name was Guegalott, Eglost Guegalott (ph). I'll never forget that -- those people, they're elderly and, I tell you, were beautiful people. Boy, I never forgot them when I was a little boy.

So what happened, after that my mother come home. Somehow, I don't know what happened to my father, but he'd still, you know, been bumming around and he was still drinking. So one day my mother come home. She had to do something with -- to take care of the kids. And my sister, Helen, she got a job in Swift and Company. But she was a couple years older than I was. We'd gotten a little older. So what happened, my mother got boiling water. She threw it on my father, then she called -- then they got the police over. And they -- of course, my mother couldn't speak English. So there was -- there was Nobinski (ph) was there, a detective, and -- see, my mother was named Nobinski, so he knew my mother. He said, "We're going to lock him up for four or five months to try to dry him out," you know, so he wouldn't drink no more.

Boy, I tell you, when he come back, he went to work for Million Hearts. He was good for about -- oh, about eight, nine months. Started all over again. He got hit by a street car. Yeah, it was a street car. He had a fractured skull. So what happened, he laid in the hospital at Cooke County. He ran away from there and he stayed home. But he was a powerful man. He was small, strong. He could take me like, throw you.

So what happened, after that, it was -- he got cured, himself, you know. No doctors, nothing. He didn't like doctors. I don't know why. So what happened, when I got a little older, I went to St. Rosalina (ph) School. I went there for about four years. I lost three years of public school because I got four times double demotion. That's how I was -- see, I don't know. God must have been awful good _________ mind to pick up things.

See, I didn't know anything about it, but I knew all about -- actually, when I was a little kid, say 11 years old, 10, 9 years old, I used to go on a farm and work for a quarter a week. I put a lot of hours in. Then I'd bring vegetables home, sauerkraut, cabbage I used to bring. And I'd bring tomatoes and ______ pickles, onions. Stuff like that, I used to get for nothing.

See, and my father was all right again. Then when I brought the cabbage, why -- this farmer used to raise big cabbage like that (indicating). It was big. It was that big. You pick one, it's eight, nine, ten pounds. Boy, I had a big one like that. And my mother and father were grating it -- and she was to clean his toenails -- you know how they used to do in Poland, they chop, chop, they put behind his arms. He was good to me. After that he bought me ice cream. He was working, working, working.

And just -- let's see, when I got to be 16, I went to St. Rosalina School in 1931. And Father Peter O'Dwyer come up. He says -- he says -- he said, "Did you hear about God?" I says -- said, "Father, I've never seen him." Yeah, I give him the right answer. He looked at me. He said, "Sharp little kid." So I had a teacher named Sister ______. So one time I lived on 45th and Laughlin and we were shooting rabbits -- or rats that big (indicating). Oh, you should see how big they were. So one day, my brother was -- on the butt at the rifle, the .22 rifle and I was on the butt and I got hit in the chin right here (indicating). The bullet lodged here. I spit out blood and teeth. I get a beating on top from my mother. But there was a little girl in the window. If I didn't get hit, she would have got hit. I looked. I seen that little girl with blue -- pretty blonde, blue eyes. I never forget her face.

Geez, after that, I went up the step -- that's when I almost got a beating -- to call the police department. They were looking for the gun. My brother ran away. He got scared. He would hide himself for a couple of days. I don't know where he was. I was in the hospital for a month.

Now, this is -- what I'm going to tell you is a true story. They took the bullet out. They had to wait for about two weeks. Boy, I could remember when I got in there, they took a swab and they put the iodine in there and pushed right in. You think I wasn't in pain. Oh, I went like -- sweat was pouring out of me. And so what happened -- so they kept it quiet, they took the bullet out -- about a week later they took it out. But it didn't leave a big scar. They had like an electric needle. They got in there and they scraped all the bone in the wound. Well, I started throwing up blood. You know them old-fashioned basins? I had a big one filled with blood. This guy was a mason, he had both legs broke. He was working on construction and two planks splitted and busted both legs. And he was watching me.

The whole -- my sister was there, Betty, my -- I don't know -- my sister, Helen, and somebody else. They thought I was going to die. And I was still living yet. I was still breathing, you know. I don't know. They didn't put me on no machine or nothing. I know there was -- at that time they ain't got the stuff like now, see. So what happened -- now, let's see. After the -- oh, yeah. When the Father come over, they told me not to talk; move my eyes yes and no. I moved my eye. And then he said, "Open your mouth and let me put that -- don't swallow it." He put that in my mouth, "And just close your mouth; let it dissolve by itself." I fell asleep, right at the Holy Communion. I tell you, in the morning, I got up. I was looking around and the nurse come over, she goes -- I pushed the nurse away from me. She says, "Are you strong." And this mason couldn't believe this, "He pulled through all that with all that blood he threw up." I was only about 86 pounds. I wasn't big. I was skinny, you know. It must have been God that saved my life. It got to be him and nobody else. I had a reason to live for then.

And then I got a job in a lard refinery. I slept -- no, first I worked -- yeah, I worked in a lard refinery. So I worked -- no, I worked in the cafeteria for Swift and Company. Mrs. Smith and Peterson was superintendent. So one time Bill Baker, my boss, he says, "Louie, you've got to clean this hall counter. We're going to have open house Sunday so people can visit here. "You know, I spent six hours cleaning that counter, shining it and everything. Mopped the floors. Everything was shining. And Mrs. Smith was the woman that run the cafeteria and Mr. Peterson was the superintendent. So he says, "I think we'll inspect the cafeteria." He looked at everything and Mrs. Smith looked at it. "Geez, is this counter clean, I never seen it like that." Because they had that stainless steel and, boy, I buffed everything out. And then he says, "Louie, you've got a job with -- in the lard refinery." So I worked in the lard refinery.

I used to make lard, bland lard, you know, Green Bay, St. Croix, butter, all that stuff. Then I worked on the lard press. We used to put it in bleach and purify it through cloth; take the cloth off. And if not -- when you went on -- then I got in -- downstairs and there's a shipping department. And Marty Doze, my boss, I got his old check number, 1101 -- 11011. He said, "Louie, that's my check number you got." I said, "Good." You know, I was in there one month, and he says, you know, "Louie, you pick this stuff up so fast," about 31 pounds of lard and a hundred pounds of Green Bay, St. Croix, this, that, 400 pounds. I knew how to weigh everything. I knew how to figure out how to load a truck, fix -- sometimes I get a couple dollars off the trucks. Like balance it, they like it when you balance it. And I used to wheel them in; I used to roll the drums about. You know, I was strong. Then I was about 150 pounds.

And I used to eat good, boy, I would. When I'd eat, I'd eat four, five sandwiches, steak sandwiches. But I'd burn it up going up and down the floor. I kept working, working, working. And I knew this -- well, but first before I did all that junk, I went to the CCC camps during the Depression, you know. It was run by the forestry department and the rest of it was done by the Army on Saturday and Sunday. So I stayed there about three years, two months before I got in Swift and Company. So I worked there and I was the head mechanic, shop _____, building links, went to Oregon, build another link out there. Then I came back and I worked for my brother-in-law.

And then I -- he was moving out. I went back to the CCC camps. So I stayed in Michigan for a year, so I made two stripes. I was a good scalper. I knew how to plant _____ because I learned from Wisconsin, you know, and other places. And then from there, Captain -- Captain -- I mean, Mr. Holt come up and he says -- I filled out a form on the kind of work that -- I was mechanic on my last job, you know, when I worked with my brother when he moved out. I worked with him for about five or six months.

See, when I come back from Swift and Company, I didn't get my old job. So I went to -- I was working for 42 cents an hour. I worked my buns off making $100 a week. Ain't that something? And I was a good mechanic. So went I got in the CCC camps, this Mr. Holt come by me -- no, I filled a form out. They asked me what kind of work; I put down mechanic. The head of mechanic over them, he had none of the trucks fixed right. None of them was running right, nothing. Do you know how long it took me to work all those trucks? Six months I had them all running. Every one of them trucks, I put brakes, new points, new pistons. If it had -- if it was out of time, I would take the whole front -- the radiator, put a new timing chain on there. I knew everything that my brother -- I could overhaul the engine, do everything; valves, grind this, that. So at that time, they didn't have hydraulic brakes them. They had what they call _____. You had to put a brake halfway down, you clamp it and you hold it, then you raise the car up, then you -- you had to wing nut on here with a lock nut. You screw it on and you keep tightening it until it's locked. Stay -- it will stay like that. Then go to the other one. Do the same thing we did first one. Then in the back was a little different. You had to lock with a little star drill like that and you shake and expand it. Then when the brake would lock, it would release one until it's free. Then I used to adjust them. Sometimes there's no brake linings; I have to put new brake linings. They go through -- and one time the -- a colonel from Mequon, Wisconsin, yeah, he come up and he asked Captain Gernburg (ph), he said, "Geez you've got a good mechanic here." He says, "Yeah, we've got the best damn mechanic in this CCC camp here."

I used about to go over to Baldwin where they overhauled the engines. See, I liked to go in there, I could overhaul a whole engine. Captain just said, "Yeah" -- because I used to fix his car, tune it up and everything. He said, "We've got" -- he said, "Bring it over." So that Sunday, I opened the Fourth Street Truck and Garage, opened it in there. Geez, I looked at the housing on the camshaft with a _____, with no grease, had broke in half; that was broken. Brake line -- no brake -- the brake line was bent. Because they had a command car. I used to fix the -- see, we -- I had to save stuff to fix everything for the Army and the forestry. So I fixed all the brakes. And then they had to drive it in there. So I tested it out. I put a cloth on the seat, you know, so I wouldn't get it dirty. And this guy took it out. I said, "Take it easy on the brakes; apply them slow." He almost went out the window. And then the captain, you know, he went -- no, this major wanted me to go to Wisconsin to work on their trucks. Captain Gernburg said, "Nothing doing. He stays here. I'm not transferring this guy to no other place."

So I was there about a year. Then I found out my mother got -- my mother was in the hospital. So what I had to do, take a ship from Lennington (ph) to Milwaukee, Milwaukee to Chicago to get home. I went in the hospital and my mother died. She had a bad kidney infection. They cut her open and the blood hit the ceiling. I looked at her. I cried. She died. So I stayed for the wake. I went back to CCC. I stopped -- see, I went and worked, worked them. Then they -- Swift and Company called me to go to work. So I went to work there and then I worked three months, I got laid off. I was a punch press operator. I worked in a gun factory. Oh, you name it, I did so many different works. Laid off, laid off, laid off. Couldn't get a steady job. Boy, after that, I was so disgusted, I didn't know what to do. That's when the war broke out. Then I got the job in the lard refinery. And then I worked there for about seven years, then I was all right. I thought I'd never get laid off. I thought they wouldn't fire me, you know, going in the Army.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: Do you remember how old were you when the war broke out?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: Yeah. About 2- -- about 23 or 24 years old. So what happened, the guy at the draft board, I knew him. He said, "Hey, Louie you better enlist in the Army you are getting drafted in two weeks." He said, "Go and get your money from Swift and Company, your vacation." Yeah, I got $80, I remember it. No, $40 -- it wasn't $80, boy, it come in handy in the Army. So I got in the Army, but I wouldn't tell anybody I had that much money on me.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: Were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: No. I enlisted. I volunteered, but I wasn't drafted. See, I volunteered. See -- so this -- the guy at the draft board, he said, "Louie, you're in charge of 45 guys." He said, "You've got a lot of experience from the Army in the CCC camps." See that's where it come in handy. And I told the guys, "Don't try to drink any whiskey or beer or anything or put soap on your arms so you get high blood pressure; they're going to keep you overnight. You ain't going to fool the doctor. The only way they won't take you is if you have a broken arm and it's healed and -- you've got to be one solid piece." The doctor, when he examined me, the only thing I didn't like, when -- he went in my ear and he made it bleed. And the major hollered at that doctor. He said, "If I ever catch you doing that again," he said, "Now, you fix that." You know, he pulled the wax out instead of washing it out and he made it bleed. He put a scar in there. So when I went in the Army up in Camp Grant -- you know, I was all right. I could hear good at that time. So from there -- let's see. They send me to -- yeah, went from Camp Grant. That's when -- then I went to Fort Sheridan to Camp Grant. From Camp Grant, I went to Camp Barkley, Texas. I was with the 45 infantry. There was a medical corp outfit. And I was there for about -- no, we had to go take three months of training. Oh, I went through obstacles. See, I was strong. Nothing bothered me. My feet didn't bother me. I used to take guys on a hike. We'd see guys with blisters and blood on their feet, tired, exhausted. The guys would say, "Geez, Louie, ain't you tired." I said, "No. Why? That's the trouble with you guys. You had these soft jobs and you're sitting on your can. You go out and exercise, you wouldn't have this problem." I used to go -- then they transferred me to Baton Rouge, Louisiana. I will never forget that town. Hot, stinking hot and the 98-degree humidity. One day, the buck sergeant come over -- he was a hillbilly, you know. And he was a nice guy, but I didn't pay no attention to him. He said, "We're going on a hike." Boy, did he get his can chewed out. Oh, God. The doctor hollered at him. He said, "If I ever catch you taking guys in 98" -- and the humidity, was so wet and hot. But everybody come back. You know, I had to walk back to get the ambulance to carry the guys in the ambulance. Feet were all bloodied from walking. Oh, boy.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: Was it part of the training?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: Yeah, it was part of the training. The second night -- the second -- I was strong. Nothing bothered me. I would haul the ambulance, come back, picked the other guys up, picked the other -- then I come back. We had like races out there. I used to go to the races and everything. Geez, the guys said, "You're fast," because I'm short body, long legs. Yeah, I've got long legs. You can see. Here's my legs; look how short my body. See.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: And, boy, I was fast. I had good lungs. I didn't smoke. Geez, I used to bash the guys up. One kid beat me. He was -- he was a funny guy. He was like a lady -- a lady's man, you know. He was -- I don't like to call him a queer, but that's the way he sounded. He looked to me like -- but he could run. Boy, that guy was faster than I was. And I didn't pay no attention after that. And then one time, he says -- the captain says, "Louie, you're going to drive Colonel Kuntz and his wife here and there, you'll take them here to there." So I used to take them to town and all. I'd clean a command car, hose a -- it was four-door sedan and I'd clean it and wash it, clean it, vacuum it. I'd clean the motor, change the oil. I used to do everything to them. He says -- and the colonel says -- he said, "Private Budz?" I said, "Yes, sir." He said, "I've never seen a car look so clean." I laughed. I just laughed, too. I says -- see, I was taught up -- I was brought up that way. That's the way my mother taught me, to stay clean. Because if you don't stay clean, you are going to be sick all your life. I never had a sick day in life until I got in the Army. I never had a cold, nothing. I always ate good.

My mother had barley soup, beef soup, sauerkraut, Polish sausage. And when I used to work, she'd make me a salami sandwich, even though when I was a little boy. When I was 16 years, I was working on a WPA project, you know. Then that's when -- that's when the jobs are -- you know, like Roosevelt, President Roosevelt, opened up their -- we used to clean up ditches, railroad, everything. So when I got in the Army, then I had some more training. Then I drove the ambulance. Now, one day, I got out a command car, drove the command car. I drove four guys, had to take a crash boat to a -- on the Mississippi River. I rode that Mississippi 22 miles. You could see the colored guys fishing for catfish, alligators. You see everything on it.

So what happened, right after that, they were going to AWOL me. I come up to the captain, I said, "Captain, I can't help it. The lieutenant was the one that kept me overnight at that crash boat out in the other lock. Because, you know, when they fill the water, they fill the other one and then they bring it and then they lower the lock. You see what I mean? It goes up and down like the Panama Canal. So I told him, you know, Call up the lieutenant. You'll find out." He was right and I didn't like the captain. Oh, I had no use for him. So one day, one boy in our outfit, his wife died and she lived 65 miles from where we were at. I told him, "I've got five bucks. You can -- do you think that's enough?" He said, "Louie, just give me three." I said, "Take the five bucks. See your mother." You know, that captain wouldn't let him go. So I took -- told Colonel Kuntz about it. That's what did it. Boy, did he get chewed out. He said, "Captain, when any of these kids die that live close by, you give them a pass and make sure he sees his mother -- and see that she gets buried." After about a month, he didn't -- he found I was the one that got him in trouble. You know what he did? He shipped me out. I thought I was going to the Pacific. I went to North Africa.

I went to Fort Dix -- Camp Kilmer, New Jersey, in New Jersey and from there I was going over to -- then I had a captain that was my medical officer and I was attached with him. And we had 10 other -- six other guys besides me. But them six guys wasn't worth a dime. But after we got in, we loaded up on a boat. John Eriksen, I'll never forget that boat, with all the GIs piling in there; A deck, B deck, C deck. They have to take off their shoes. Stink. Smell that. Gosh. Oh, boy, that's tough. And you don't take a bath. You eat two days -- two meals a day, breakfast and supper. They give you a lot of dry foods and always feed you something heavy to stick with you. And then towards about -- towards about 4:00 or 5:00 o'clock, then you get a good dinner, like whatever they make you eat, like meat, potatoes, veal, this, that, soup, vegetables and fruit. And you could take the fruit with you that you could eat, you know. And then I never slept inside of the boat. I slept on top of the deck. I had my blanket and wrapped myself up because it's stuffy down there. You couldn't stand the smell in there. You don't take a shower. Only so many people go in there take a shower at a time. You don't take a shower for three weeks, you smell of salt. Sweat's coming out of you.

Then they says -- when they load us on the boat, the guys told us, "You are going to North Africa." I thought this was a military secret. They all knew about it. Oh, man. What happened, I landed in Casablanca. And we had all our equipment on that big ship, you know, I was on. And there was other ships besides that that hauled that -- you know, our material, our stuff, our trucks, you know, everything, the rifles, the guns and everything. So I landed in Casablanca and there was nobody to operate the big crane. I said, "Well, let me go up to take a look at it." I said, "Captain" -- I told the doctor. I went upstairs, I looked. Says power on. And I couldn't read French but I moved the lever and it moved this way, then I moved it the other way, this way, go that. Then I learned how to raise the cables to pick up the equipment, how to tie it up and it will go up and how to push that -- that whole thing on the trailer tractor that carry it on the trucks, a two-and-a-half-ton truck. I was so good at it, I moved all the equipment. Then the major said, "This is an order. You will move it." I said, "Look, I've got orders to take my mission and," I said, "you bring a kid over and I'll teach him how to operate this." He said, "I ain't got time." "Well, you're going to have time because I'm leaving." I said, "That's my captain, there's my major and," I says, "I can't take orders from you. He is the one I take orders from. And I got to go up to them and I'm in the medical corp and I've got to get out of here and I can't stay here." I said, "What if somebody gets killed or wounded? Are you going to take care of them?" Boy, he shut up all of a sudden. I left. Shit, I left.

And then we moved up to -- let's see, what the hell was name of that first town? Oh, the French fort -- the French fort out there, we moved out there, and then we had to go to the Kassapian Pass. Boy, you should see the tanks. We were all shot up, all American tanks, by the Germans 88. I'll never forget that. After that, we were moving up closer, closer, closer. I could remember -- let's see. Constantine, then I went to Algiers -- no, Bazetti was the last stop. No, Tunis -- no, Constantine, Tunis, then I go to -- what the heck. I can't think of that little town. It was nothing but a desert out there. The -- so one time we were bivouacking the area and the British soldiers were there. They told us, "You better watch your guns, barracks, backs. There's nobody living out there. Nobody." And one night the guys fell asleep. And we had guards out there. See, the people, like Arabs, they lived in the holes out there. You won't believe it. They stole the guys' guns, rifles, everything. Boy, oh, boy, I couldn't believe it. Good thing I slept with everything on top of me. I didn't have no rifle or nothing. See, I was in medical and I couldn't carry a gun. And when I found out, hey, I'm going to carry a gun. I don't know when I'm going to get shot. So when I got into Tunis, then I had a big .38. Boy, I had a whole pack of ammunition. I had two clips, put one in the bag, you know, and it was right lying next to me. And the gun was always by me. Never -- never -- I mean, driving the trucks, I put my hand on the gun and go driving. And then the Germans were starting to surrender. That's when Rommel was getting -- you know, getting pushed back, pushed back. The Germans were something. Good thing he speaked English. And I had the gun cocked. Oh, I was -- I wasn't scared, but you never knew what they were going to do. And he asked me -- I says, "Yeah, well, keep your hands up because I'll shoot you." He says, You're not supposed to carry." I says, "I don't give a shit. You are SS."
A lot soldiers that -- that they didn't make off their -- you know, they didn't have no guns, but they killed them. They massacred a whole bunch in Malmedy in Germany [sic].

So what happened, after I said, "You walk about five miles and report to the M.P. station." So I'm looking through the window, I'm still having the gun, I'm looking, driving, driving until I got about four blocks away. Then I knew. I left. Then I got into Tunis and that's when I told you about that Alfred O'Shelago (ph). The stuka dive bomber fell on him. And I told the guys, "What choice do we got here?" We could have pulled him out." But what you do, he's shot in the spinal cord. The doctor asked me, he said, "Captain, says" -- see, we had six other guys when we got rid of them. They transferred them. He only wanted two people, the sergeants, Charlie and me. So what happened, I put the knife on his leg. I said, "Al, do you feel what I'm" -- he says, "No." So what happened, we had to take him to a British hospital and they had to make a special cast, you know, for his leg. But I had to change the kidney solution. See, I was the only medical technician within 75 or 80 miles.

We used to take care of the _______, Italians and so on, everybody. Even the soldiers, the colored people we used to take care of. Oh, everybody. For typhus, this, that. Like for malaria, you rush them to the hospital with malaria. And after that, after three days at the fort, we went back to Tunis. There on the airfield I couldn't see. It was pitch black out there at nighttime. But the general -- a certain general kind of looked at my eyes. He says, "When did you sleep last, soldier?" I said, "Sir, this is the fourth night I'm pulling duty. This is the fifth -- fourth night I haven't slept. I've got to pull my duty. I got nobody. I'm the medical technician ______."

Boy, he got hysterical. Five minutes, then another ambulance come. He says, "You go see a doctor; give you one-fourth of a gram of codeine." The next morning, I couldn't open my eyes. They were closed solid. I was blind. I put cold water -- how could you get cold water when it's so warm, 80, 80, 90, 95. I remember when I was in Cape Bottoms (ph), it was 117 hot. The guys were passing out. One guy had malaria bad. Oh, God. He said, "Louie, close that window. It's cold." I says, "Take your combat shoes off." I had to untie my shoes and put the sweat out. My whole uniform that was brown was all white with salt. You had to eat on the hour, on the hour and drink hot water.

I got to Rabat; that's where the hospital was. I dropped him off. And then I was hungry that day. I said -- I don't give a shit how hot it was. I'd eat anything cold or hot. I asked the doc, "Do you have any ice water?" He grabbed me and said, "Soldier, come here," and give me hot coffee. I said, "I haven't eaten good for two or three days." He said, "Come on." We went to the hospital. They had meat, potatoes, ketchup, sauerkraut. Boy, did I eat. I ate so much, I couldn't drive.

Then I used to know a guy that had his arm blown off. In Tunis, I took him to Rabat. I had to take care of his arm, and I asked, I said -- you know, look at him, keep up -- keep the bandage up. Then I met some British captains, soldiers _____; they give you a fifth of White Horse scotch whiskey. Boy, held that back. So I slipped in a tent with blankets. Oh, the blankets were so high -- see, the nights are cold in Africa. So what happened, I got in the blanket and I slept there. Geez, I slept so late. Then I was waiting for another flight that was going to Tunis. I got on a C-47, and before I got halfway to Tunis one of the engines went out. Yeah, it just stopped going. The C-47 is the safest plane. This guy come in with that one engine short. This guy Connolly -- Connors comes up and he says, "What the hell are you doing on a plane?" I said, "I had to take a guy to Rabat." He said, "Did you know?" I said, "Yeah, I seen it out the window." He said, "Were you scared?" I said, "I ain't going to live forever." You know, you're young. You don't care. Geez, I'll never forget that. Then when I got back to -- went back to visit him. So one day I wanted to take a shower. There was no fresh water nowhere, so I went to the new basarti (ph). There was a place where the troops were at. That was in Corsica, too. I stayed there for two weeks because -- see, before we -- before we -- before I got into Corsica, but first we was going to hit that beach in Salerno, see. So what happened, I got at the -- no, I went and dove in that water. Boy, I was washing that saltwater. My hair was stiff. I was itching from the salt, skin. My whole body was -- so I didn't have nothing to rinse it off. I said, "Hell, I'll sweat it out." So I was drinking water. It was hot. Oh, then I started sweating. But you smell.

They eat them C rations. You can't cook, you know. See, you use that helmet for everything. We wash in it, cook our eggs. And if you got to go potty, you go potty. That thing stunk, I'm not kidding you. ________+. You know, I used to drive the Jeep. One day the guy says, "Where the hell did you get your hot water, Louie?" He says _______+. I had that soluble coffee. We called it varnish remover. You poured that in there. He said, "Hey, Louie, what" -- I said, "For Christ sake, you stupid fool. You've got a canteen. Put a match stick on it and put it on the manifold and motor for five miles, you get hot water. You can't put your hands on. You have to get a pair of gloves." Boy, that end there. And you get that cream, that's that powder cream, you pour it in and, boy -- the captain said -- see, a lot of guys used it for hot water and shaving and everything. He says, "Geez" -- and the major says, "Boy, that Budz, he knows a lot of things we don't know about."

You know, I used to be so good when I was in the stockyards, there was big steamers like that. I used to throw it in the fence right -- a big fence they had. I used to _______+ with the sticker. I used to stick it with a point. See, it was a round circle and it was a _____ that long. We done chopped up that whole fence with that ______. I was good at throwing things, you know. It come in handy some day. You never know when you're going to use it. Throw something or throw a spear at a guy or something. You've got to learn how to handle it. I used to throw dice like that, though. I used to learn a lot of things. I was not lazy. But I always kept thinking about the war. When am I going to get it. He said, "Don't worry." Everything he said, "Do not worry. Do not worry." It was put into my mind, the way you crack up, that's true. And I believe it.

Then we hit Salerno. God almighty. That's when things started. All hell broke loose. I can remember I was in the Jeep with the Red Cross helmet. I put the ______ on the carburetor and manifold and hyperextension. I wired all the spark plug wires. I had to wire the carburetor, this, that and the alternator. And then we drove right in saltwater coming out and, geez, was I soaking wet with saltwater again. I hit the beach, and the guys said, "______ Come out from the sun," and everybody ran for the beach. I jumped out of the Jeep. I left the Jeep, you know, at the beach there. I couldn't get out. I jumped out of it and I hit the -- then the bullets were boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. I says, "Heaven and hell, here I come." Boy, I was lucky. Nobody got wounded. Nobody got wounded. But then the guys with the ak-ak gun, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. You could hear it. I don't know if they got the plane or not, but they didn't stay that long, I know for sure.

And then I went in 1944 -- '43, '44 -- 19- -- it was when Mount Vesuvius was erupting. We stayed in this little town called Seille near Pompeii and we were watching that. Mount Vesuvius was erupting. Boy, you should see that lava coming down. And the lightning was striking so. Then they had a cyclone, tornado. It was close to the evening. You could see that cyclone, just sucking water, that saltwater in the air. And the ambulances were going like this. Puppets was flying, everything. I laid out -- I laid on the floor. You put your hand up, you could touch the lightning. That's how close it was. God must have been with me or my guardian angel, whoever was there. I'll never forget that, God almighty.

So what happened after that, the next day when the lava stopped flowing and then we -- anyway, then I -- we found the bivouac area, so we set up the tent supply. We had to put a small tent, not a big one. But the other guys, they transferred, you know. He didn't want them. The doctor didn't want those guys along. They wasn't good for nothing. So the doctor kept me because I knew how to do a lot of things. So what happened, after they got rid of them, he says, "Louie, we are going to have to do this ourselves." I said, "It don't bother me, Doc."

But I remember we took a German microscope from Tunis there. It was on the German -- from a guy for a dentist and all. So we took that, so we used that for our own use. You could tell by the blood whoever got malaria disease or got syphilis or gonorrhea or stuff like that. Boy, I tell you one damn thing, the people, they used to keep me busy all the time. In the medical corp, you are on the go constantly. You get a guy with a brain spouting out; he's got a piece of shrapnel. I had to take care of him and rush him to the doctor putting gauze on him. I said, "Doc, I've got a rush. He got hit with a piece of shrapnel." He says, "Rush him." I took him on down _____ as fast as the ambulance can go, come back again. And everybody else that's sick that was mild, I didn't care about the guys. I drive slowly, I drove 40 miles, 30 miles to get them to the hospital, let them do that. See, it is a station hospital where they take care of you. But when you have a battle aid station, they fix the guys one, two, three. I carried a guy one time at the battle aid station, I carried a guy in there. I don't know what was wrong with him. I could see German soldiers with hypodermic needles in their chest so they can breathe. Yeah, you'd be surprised. I asked the guy, "What -- what happened?" Then the guy was showing us pictures about the Holocaust. And some of the Germans, boy, they didn't like -- they didn't like what Hitler was doing after he was killing all those people. And then I seen those pictures in Italy. There was a tanker with a cab on it and it was smuggled out. I don't know how the guy got out of there. Boy, it was a terrible sight to see those people --

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: Was it the first time you were aware that this happened --

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: -- through the pictures?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: Yeah. Boy, I tell you one thing. It was a terrible sight. You get sick. The only thing I'd get -- I worried about all them soldiers. They died fighting for your country. You people don't give a damn about the soldiers. They were living out there. And sometimes I wished I was living with them, with those soldiers. Then my problems would be over. Boy, I tell you, God was awful good to me to come home in one piece. I don't know. I just can't tell you why. But the other reason, I would go out of my way to save a life. I can remember one time a British soldier hit a pillar and the guy's leg was mangled so bad. When I had to care of this guy, the doctor took care -- he said, "Louie, help me put a splint on because I don't know how." So I put that on. And the Surgeon General looked at it. He said, "You guys are on the hall." The British soldier with the busted leg -- I didn't have no plasma. See, I couldn't give plasma. The doctor does that, at that time, see. But I know how to give shots, needles, stuff like that. He died. Yeah, I saved the other guy's life. He was -- he was fighting for the same cause we were. Then _____+ I went to France, I went to Dijon. We made a diversion; I unloaded in there. And then I went to Frankfurt, to the Darmstadt and I was near Aachen. I went to Cologne, _____+, Munich. Munich I used to call Munchkin and Munkin. Then I got into Australia -- Austria. I stayed there when the war was all over with. But there's still a lot of stories I could tell you from behind. The only thing, the white crosses, even from World War I. I looked at every one of those crosses and the tears were coming out of my eyes. Even in Korea, the war they were fighting. The Koreans, the same way. I see all the GIs were shot up dead and the guys were picking up and throwing them on the truck like two-by-fours. Then I made the sign of the cross. I didn't want to cry no more. I wanted to quit worrying. They didn't get back to the front lines again. They always start pushing, pushing, pushing, pushing. And then we got up to Seoul and they start pushing us back. Do you want to shut it off?

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: The tape is over. END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: Then I got -- see, I got out of the Army in 1945. Oh, there's a lot of stories I could tell you. But see, I can't remember all of it, but what I done, you know. Most of this stuff, like in Africa, Sicily, Italy, oh, crud. I went to Rome, stayed there in Rome. Stayed there one week and moved on. Then that battle at the _____, that's a long battle. A lot of people were lost there. They had to get the dead off the field. So I was stuck with dead bodies. A human body smelled bad. I used to go on autopsy cases, guys would get shot. I told the doc, "Come over this side." He says, "Why?" I said, "The wind's blowing that way. We won't smell it." He looked at me, "You're smart." I said, "Doc, I know what I'm talking about. We see enough in this here." I found a guy in Tunis like -- it's happened -- yeah, Tunis somewhere. Every time I drove by, I smelled a body. I smelled -- I had a good nose at that time. Doc said, "Are you sure, Louie?" I said, "I know. Can't you smell it?" He says, "No." I seen the road -- I don't know if it was mud or not -- I said, "Do you want to take the gravel?" He said, "Let's go." So we drove on the gravel road. And right where we was, we seen a guy laying that the Arabs cut the parachute off. And we found -- I found a piece of ______, a bramble bush and I give it to the doctor. And we found it. Good thing I had alcohol. See, that would wash his hands. And then I had a gauze to wipe the maggots off. And then he washed, I washed my hands. We rinsed it out. And it was -- and it was this Will Smith, William Smith of North Carolina. He was missing in action for about -- oh, about four, five months. Yeah, he was there about four months in Africa. _____+. Then when I got discharged from the Army, I was telling you about that guy O'Shelago (ph). The doctor come over -- he called me up. I stayed about 40, 50 -- no, I lived here, but my sister had a house at that time -- see, that's when I -- so I was bored and I had to go to Ohio, take care of my nieces and nephew because my brother's wife died with cancer. So I took care of them for six -- I got bored staying home. So I went back in again. And the doctor called me. He said, "Louie, remember the guy you picked up" -- see, I had a '51 Chevy at that time. I said, "Yeah, I know where he lives." I said, "Do you want to see him?" He says, "Yeah, come on." So I took him. He was at the Cooke County Hospital. He was a specialist, a baby doctor. He used to tell me, "You'd make a good doctor. Boy, you know a lot." So what happened, he got in the hospital -- I mean, _____ over on 68th and Green Street, walked in and we found a rat. He said, "Louie, you're right." I said, "Yeah, I know. I'm always right. You know that yourself, Doc." He laughed at me. I says, "Okay," I said, "Doc," I said, "Are you hungry? I didn't eat no supper." We met Mr. and Mrs. O'Shelago. Now, the funny part about it, about this soldier Al, you know, he got married. He got married and that girl must have loved him. And he was furloughed. So after we got the conversation, we started about 15 minutes, I says, "Doc," I says, "Do you like barbecue ribs?" He said, "Boy, I love them." "Come on, I'll take you to a place I know on Wallace." On 29th and Wallace, there was a guy who specialized in them. I took him there. I could have taken him to the Stockyards, you know, for a good steak dinner, but he said he loved barbecue. You know, he ate the whole big thing. I said, "Boy, you've got an appetite, Doc." Oh, he liked me. I liked him, too. He was from Athens, Ohio. And I never kept in touch with him. I don't know what happened -- he's -- oh, I betcha he's gone by now. Because I'm 86. Yeah, he's gone. He was older than I. He was about 40 at that time. Yeah, he's gone. He was a good doctor, though. You know, his father-in-law put him in college. He was 17 years old. He spent close to 25, 30 years to be a good doctor, and he was good. He knew how to get a sinus infection I had in Germany. Boy, put that stuff that they use for gonorrhea, that ardual (ph). They put that in my nose. You put three big drops. And he says, "Stay right there." And it was burning and burning. Voom, when I blew it out, you should seen the pus, blood, everything, the infection come out of there. Then he washed it out with distilled water. A couple days later, I could breathe again. Boy, I was normal. And then when I got in the Army, then I was catching colds left and right. This was cold, that. When I took -- you know, I was in the medical. I could get the whole -- the antihistamine tablets, what I need. _____+ that was sick. You know, a lot of people got sick. I used to -- the guy from Texas, the cook, I said, "Better make some chicken soup for ringworm." He was our cook and he was good. I took care of them. I said, "Doc, Primo's got a big fever; he's got about 104." He said, "Louie, go get the Campho-phenique." I said, "Yes, sir." I opened the safe up, got the Campho-phenique. We gave him one in the morning and one in the noon and one at -- and then I says, "Wait a minute, Doc. I've got to get some blankets." We made some hot soup. I think we had hot coffee. I wrapped him up in blankets. Boy, did he sweat. Stuff was coming out of him, water, everything. Right after we got him well, he went to the kitchen. He said, "Louie, and you, Dr. Alsadro (ph)," he says, "I'm going to fix you guys good dinner." Boy, he made chicken for us. Was it good. That's the first time we had a good hot meal, you know, instead of eating the sea ration cans.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: After how long?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: Huh? Well, we stayed there for about -- well, that was -- what's the -- Corsica -- in Corsica -- no, that was in Corsica. It's got to be in Italy, it was. It was in Italy, yeah. And that's when he got well. So sometimes the Italian peoples would come up there. They get them half pound T and Ts waterproof. They go out in the ocean and, geez, they come back with a lot of fish. See, they give us a whole case of fish. Boy, we had fish for -- for that -- for dinner for the 200 guys we had. Gee, it was the first time we had fish for so long. Then we found a place in New Albatelo, a big ammo dump. It was loaded with bombs. I used to go up there to look up there and I seen crates and everything. I told the doctor, I said, "Doc," I said, "I know we ain't got no crates for our medicine and stuff." We always carried it in boxes. He said, "If they're good crates, bring some back." And I was going in the ambulance to get some. See, at that time, nobody was wounded or hurt. So I went -- I went there and this one guy says, "Hey, Louie, get the" -- he swore at me. I said, "Get the hell out of this place. It's going to go up." You should see what happened. It was a mile and a half we were away from -- and I told the doc, I said, "Doc, watch over there. You see what's going to happen." I said -- you know, I said "Yadro and his Jesse James gang," they blew up that ammunition dump. You know how high it went? 20,000 feet in the air. That's how -- that stuff was supposed to go to the French. The major was pulling his hair out and he had no hair left to pull. He was like -- in Naples, the _______ was so bad and I forgot to put my helmet on, but I said not any coming, but they come close. I hear it coming, but I ducked and it was right close by me. Then the kid on the other mountain, he had his helmet on. And the ack-acks were going -- like you can walk on it. That's how thick it was. And the kids holler, "There goes my old man's war bonds." You have to laugh. If you don't laugh, you'll crack up. Oh, shit. I'll never forget that. Sometimes there were good parts, sometimes bad parts. I had my cousins from Pennsylvania come to visit me in Foglia. They were in Foglia. I was on the other side of Naples. I'll never forget they come over, Andy and Frank. Well, Frank, he looked like me almost. Geez -- and I had some sunglasses by -- that were used by the airport -- you know, fighter pilot. I found a pair by a fighter plane. And they -- he come over. I says -- I says, "Hey, Frank, would you want Air Force glasses?" He said, "Geez, yeah, I like them. They're nice." I give them to him. It wasn't nothing. Then -- and a girl from Pennsylvania sent me three cans of beer and they were Hornig (ph). And then Charlie, me and my doctor, I said, "Doc, do you like beer?" He says, "Yeah." I give him a can and Charlie got a can. And he is from Pennsylvania and he loved the same beer I give him. Boy, we're drinking and sipping it like you'd never seen beer in your life. Oh, geez. Sometimes you had a good time. Sometimes you are on the constant go, go, go, go, go, go, go. Never stop. Go, go, go, go. Somebody gets hurt. Go. Take them to the hospital, backing you up. Pick us up another guy. Go, go, go. Then we got almost -- when the war was about getting all over with -- like I told you, I was in the Black Forest. The bullets were flying all over. And not one bullet hit the ambulance. Not one. The guy who should have been -- yeah, it was a good thing. I looked all over the ambulance. Not one bullet hole. And I told the guy, I said, "For Christ sake, will you -- what the hell is going on?" He said, "The war's over." Boy, was I happy. Shit, I was so happy. Then we got -- we had to stay in the small towns, you know, to keep an observation on the people. They were very nice to us, especially the Germans, Polish, there was mixed, Ukraines. A lot of people was there. So what happened, the one woman come over -- the doctor was in the office and Charlie come over. I said, "Charlie, hey, come over. What's she talking about? What's she saying? Her son's sick?" I said, "Doc, she said -- told Charlie that the son is sick." I said, "What should I do?" He said, "I'll take the ambulance and we'll go see what he looks like." Here I find the kid had an appendicitis, so I took the right leg, I put it up this way by him and I put that foot there and I laid him on the stretcher. And I said, "You stay still like that. No move." But somebody had to hold the leg because he might go back again. See, that eases the pain. You know, I got him in the hospital just in time. He would have died. He had a ruptured appendix. It broke right in the hospital when we operated on him. And then I met a beautiful German girl, a nurse. She knew how to talk English, you know. Then I showed her -- like one kid was stealing gas and he got shot in the hand, so I give him some morphine. See, it's a soret. You take the lid off, shoot them, wash it off, shoot them. I told the nurse, "I gave him half of that stuff. Tell the doctor." and he put the sling so he wouldn't be in so pain. So -- so I go back and forth to look at that kid, see how he was doing, you know. He should never steal gas. And I told him -- told him in German, said, "Don't do that. They're ordering to shoot to kill even." It was a good thing he was young. So what happened, she got to liking me. She was a pretty girl, though. But the only trouble is we moved out. And then I had a small girlfriend named Hildegard. I used to save candy bars and everything. And a lot of those German soldiers, they didn't care much for Hitler. She says, "Louie, do you think you can get cigarettes?" I said, "Yeah, wait, I'll go see if the guys, if they got any." I said, "Anybody got cigarettes for sale? I'll buy them off you." You know, some guys didn't smoke. I bought four cartons, you know, big ones. I brought them to the hospital. I told the nurse, "If you do it, don't give them the whole pack. You give them one at a time to every one of them. They'll last longer. If you give them all, they'll smoke them like fast." She said, "I'll do it that way." She said, "Where are you from?" I said, "From Chicago." She said, "That's a gangster town." Yeah, it is a gangster town, but I don't -- I'm not a gangster. I wouldn't have gotten involved. She was very pretty. I liked her very much. I tell you what, I would have married her. She was Catholic. So we went to church in Wiesbaden there. That's the town where I was at. Oh, I was in Darmstadt, little -- small little towns. Oh, a lot of small towns. Saarland, Stuttgart. So what happened -- if we didn't move, that's the only thing that -- I was disappointed. And I forgot to get her address. I would have married her. But I tell you what, German people are good people, just like the Polish. They know how to clean a house good. One time I went to a house; it was spic and span. Not even dust, dirt or anything. I used to find a lot of marks all on the wall, ceiling that had dropped. It was marks or shoulder marks. They were no good. It's inflation money. They left a lot of stuff there. We were down in the cellar. We found pickles, pickled beets, this, that, potatoes, everything. Boy, put it in our hands, eating the stuff. But, you know, you don't eat no vegetable, fresh stuff. But then, after that, we started getting better meals, you know, like home cooked meals. But the Army, you know how it is. Did you ever eat what they call -- I hear this -- it is called shit on shingles. Do you know what that is? Creamed beef with toast. Is that good. So you take milk, put that -- cook the beef first, put a little salt, pepper, make your toast good and thick, brown it and pour it on. Ooh, is that good. Oh, I used to love that. Geez, we used to have a name for everything.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: So how long did you stay after the war was over?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: Well, the war was over in about 38 months. I think it was 38 months, didn't I tell you? Let me see. Let's see. Forest serviced eight months and 19 days -- oh, that's longer than that. Let's see. I got out in '45. That's 24 months -- 32 months and 19 days. That's how long I'd been in there. So that's tetanus, typhoid, small pox. See, I go home with $140. Captain Riesman --

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: Do you remember -- what was the biggest act of courage that you saw by an ally or by an enemy?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: You mean, when I went to Korea? I reenlisted again after I was home a year and a half, see, when I was about 30 -- almost -- it was almost 30 years old. 29 or 30 years old. See, I was going to put in 20 years. I had -- I had three years already, then I had five years. I would have retired at 50. And that's when I got sick. I was in combat for five weeks. Tell you something, that Korean conflict did a lot of damn things to me, damaged my whole life, malaria, Germany malaria I had, sick, coughing blood and disease -- malaria again. The doctor told me I had 105.6 and should have been dead. He said, "I don't know how you got out of there alive." Then they moved me to Brooks Army hospital in San Antone, Texas. I was there for three months. Oh, I was like this. I couldn't eat. I had -- throwing up like -- threw up 'til my guts. See, I drank that rice paddy water. It was on top. There was a woman was drinking it and I thought it was fresh water, but it wasn't. I had no halazone tablets to purify the water. And the water was covered and I drank some. You know, four or five guy -- three, four guys died from that and I pulled through. I was real lucky. So what happened, I got a hallucination and that's when they put me in the psychiatric -- I said, "Look, I'm not that crazy." I said, "I know what I'm doing." I told the guy -- the doctor, you know the psychiatrist. I said, "You want me to take a test? I'll take a test." He said, "No, you're pretty normal," he said. So I had to go to the hospital where they took me. But I had a doctor -- Captain Woods was the doctor that took care of me all those months I was in there. I couldn't eat nothing, oh, for about two -- they made me drink medicine, like ether, to burn that infection that's inside, but it won't hurt you. I said -- I said, "If I don't wake up, I don't wake up." I don't know. When you're sick, you don't care to live. But then the doctor was smart. He says, "Corporal, this is an order." I never disobeyed orders. He said, "You go to mess hall to the diet class and you eat. I don't care what you eat, but eat. I want you to eat a good meal. That's an order. If you don't, I'm going to watch you, because I'll have somebody tell me about you." Because I told -- he was smart. He knew what he was doing. So I ate. I threw it all up. Same thing the second day. I had -- I ate three meals a day. The third day, then it dawned on me. Now, I knew why he did that. When I threw up, I had some stuff left in my stomach. You see how smart he was? Then I told the doctor, "Yeah," I said, "you're pretty sharp, Doc. You're smart. You told me I threw up half, but you leave there -- but, geez, I had to go to the toilet for about two weeks or they give me an enema. You don't want to be in that room when I went -- I had to go to the toilet. Ooh, I couldn't stand the smell of it. Because, you know, you are so constipated. I couldn't move my bowels, it was so hard. But then later on, then I started eating normally, I feel -- I was still like this, shaking, shaking. But he says, "Louie, we're going to send you home." Then I had to go before the evaluation board. You know that's when they asked me everything in Korea. So what happened, it got reported -- I was supposed to have gotten -- have a representative from the American Legion. I had to do all the talking. I said, "You are nothing but a dummy here." I said, "I don't need you." So I told them, I said, "Look, I love the Army. I don't want to get out. I want to stay in." I said, "I want to make a career out of the Army." They said, "Corporal Budz, you're through. You're through with the Army, fighting, everything. You've got to go home on a disability." But then later on they told me I was -- when I got home -- see, I was deferred to duty. See, marked deferred to military service. See. No, they wouldn't take me. That's when I get -- see [reading], explain reciprocation, stress, severe combat in Korea, the personality area, difficult early life, reserve combat experience, ______+, conscientious, degree of something, incapacity, part deferral of military service. They wouldn't take me. I was trying to go back in and I couldn't. Yeah, I liked the Army, I sure did. They said [reading] Discharged honorable -- five years honorable service, 1951.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: So how can you compare both wars, World War II and Korean War?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: Korean War was a filthy war. Disease, 80 percent disease. Now, World War II wasn't too bad. There was a medic guy's disease, but the only things you got to watch out, you don't eat the food from -- what the Arabs cook or something like that. You have to go to a fine restaurant. That's the only thing that was good about World War II, is that -- it was more like a clean war. But it was a terrible war. A lot of guys just tell me, like at the Battle of the Bulge or the artillery of the 88s and the Germans were good at that. They had special forces in there, Rangers, Green Berets, everything in there. They used to get blown up to pieces, legs flying, arms and everything. That's why I never stood in a fox hole. I used to dig a fox hole not far from my ambulance. My ambulance would be parked across the street and I'd dig it over here. Because you know that when they see that white cross, they'll bomb that. Sometimes the Germans are hauling ammunition in the ambulance. So the pilots had to strike. You should see how many they blew up. Now you are getting a taste of it. You see what I had to go through? I love my country. I told the president to go to hell. He took me to safety. That's what I was fighting for. See, people in Congress, they don't know what a soldier went through. These Congressmen sit on their dead can, they make money and they cheat you out of everything you got and you voted for them. They don't own -- Congress don't own the world. God owns the world, you know, everybody in it. He made a doctor, senate, president, everything. You can't take -- and they're not listening. I don't care for none of the politicians. I don't care who they are, what they are, what they look like. I'm not afraid -- I don't care what they -- they could court-martial me. They can't do nothing to me now. I live in a country where it's my right to be. The only thing I feel sorry is the kids for today. But I feel sorry for your kids if you get married. But if you do, make sure you educate them. Wish them to be computers or doctors. Doctors are the best. But you've got to be a good doctor. See, when they got doctors in the front line, sometimes they operate maybe, oh, I don't know. Some don't sleep maybe a week, two weeks. They give them -- they give them the best of everything, the food the best, best whiskey and all. So they have to drink to go to sleep. But they fix the guys up. Boy, I tell you, stitch the guys up, take the -- shave the guys, take -- make a hole, bore a hole, take the cap off, put the shrapnel, put the cap on, seal it. Don't take look for a real skilled surgeon. They're all 30, 35 years old. They're skilled and stitching people and doing everything. They learn more in the Army about doing work on a GI than anyplace else. So a guy -- get a guy that has his arm shot off, cheek shot off, head blown off, leg blown up to here. ______+. Now, none of those medical technicians that were in combat in Korea when they take the dead off the field, so they crack up, too, just looking at it every day. Some guys will. I was watching a movie, a serious movie about real combat that was taken by Army, Full Metal Combat, I was watching that. I don't know what -- what town we were in. I don't know if it was Germany or Africa or Italy. You could see the GI was like this, shaking from too much. You see too much of that stuff, you crack up.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: And what were you doing in Korea?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: Huh? Oh, I was -- I was combat infantry. All the time fighting combat. Castinago (ph). Two guys were wounded in my squad. Then the captain -- I don't know if it was a lieutenant or captain looking for the experienced veteran. I was the only one there. Yeah, a bunch of kids, 20 years old and 17, 19, 18. One kid was crying, "I want my mama." The other kid throws -- you break his arms if you move. Oh, you freeze. If you're worried, that's what happens. I told God, I said -- like the time we was going through a potato patch. The guy -- I was going to -- I was too late. I couldn't -- I was not too close to the guy with the BAR. And I said -- and he found him. They found him where he was. He was in the tree. And they -- I don't know if there was one or two guys they shot down. And this guy took a canister; it is a phosphorous. Boy, a piece of it will go right through your hand. They threw it and it was burning like the dickens. And that was it -- that was where the snipers -- bullets were coming so close to me. I was looking in the back. There's nobody back there. I looked again. Had to be somebody there. Got to be my guardian angel. It had to be somebody. So I laid in the patch -- I made like I was dead and I laid like that. Now, I was in sunlight and I had the rifle close by; I had my hand on the rifle. I don't know how I laid. I just laid there and laid there like that. I played dead. They thought I was dead, but I wasn't. Then I found out the guys were all getting up, then I got up. They start moving up again. Got to keep moving, moving, moving. You go up one hill, go down, go up another hill, go down another hill, up the other hill. You get shot at. We can shoot at them. You got to either kill or be killed. It's an order. You follow orders. Boy, is my throat getting sore. So what happened when I got out of the Army, I didn't get my old job again. No. See, I was handed a check; it was signed for $5,000. They made me do labor work. I quit. I went to another place. I worked for a sprinkler outfit, box factory, Bisking (ph) Corporation. I couldn't stand it. Swing shift. You work one week, next week in the afternoon and the next at night and I couldn't sleep right. I was losing weight. And then I worked for a box factory. Oh, I worked at so many jobs I had, I quit. Then -- then I got so disgusted, then that's when my sister-in-law died, then I went to Ohio. And I stayed there for six months to take care of the kids in Toledo, i had Jeri and Bootsie, when his wife died with a tumor. I was a pallbearer at her wake. So what happened, I said, "John, I'm going back home to Chicago. And I told my sister, "I'm going to take care of the kids. There's nobody to take care of them." That's when I left. Then I went back to Chicago. I tried to get a job. I used to be a tile setter. I worked for a building contractor. He starts cheating me out of my pay, I quit him. I said, "Bullshit, I can't get a good steady job. You get laid off no matter where you work." I joined the Army. Then I spent about a year, three years in the Army. I liked it. Oh, I was happy. I was working every day. I didn't have to worry about getting laid off or hollered at or something like that. So they fixed me up but good, but the Army did me good. It educated me. I got a lot of knowledge. You know, a lot of guys wish -- they wish they knew what I could do today. Boy, they'd know about it. In my old neighborhood when they found out I was an electrician -- a girl, you know, I used to know back, they used to call me a dummy and everything. Yeah. "Now you want me to fix your house? You're nuts. You get an electric -- licensed contractor. You are going to find out what you're going to pay." I wouldn't do nothing for nobody there. One friend of mine I did something for him, Ed Nadis (ph). He died young, drinking. The other guy died with a bullet in his spine. I'll show you who the kid is.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: Taking a short break.

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: I used to like -- his brother took out -- got his leg blown off in Omaha Beach. I had a real starched -- I had a good suit. I paid a lot of money for that suit. What the heck. I was making good money, I didn't care. He had a good job. He was working for a trucking outfit. You could tell the face was full. Big arms. You could see his shoulders. He was strong. I didn't like civilian life after that. I always wondered if I would get used to it, but I never did. Couldn't get used to it. When I was in the Army, I was at home. I was working all the time, keeping busy, doing this, doing that. Oh, shit. Drive trucks here, there, go pick up stuff, this, that, start referring -- ______, did carpentry work in there, did everything.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: I know, Louie, that you are single and what made you --

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: What made you make that decision?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: I didn't want to get married.

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: You didn't?

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: I think I told you. A guy -- a guy got to my girlfriend and that was it. Then after that, to me, the way I looked at it, women were all alike. Like you take my brother-in-law. He had four daughters. They're all looking for husbands. They're too lazy to work. Honest. Stanley's father said, "Why don't you marry" -- I said get the -- I said -- I told them, "Get your daughters to go to work. They're just looking for husbands so they could support them." You know what Stanley was doing? They used to wash his feet, his little sister. He was supporting them. He got disgusted. He married my sister. Then see how fast they all got married. But all of a sudden, the Army -- I was in Korea and my -- this Jean, my brother Walter, he got married to her. And I looked at myself. I said, "Yeah, that baby girl Linda." Then about four, five -- no, wait. I don't know how long -- how old was she but she was 6, 7 years older than Kenny. Then she had the boy and he ain't worth a dime. None of my nieces don't call you, how I felt, how I was sick or never asked me how you felt in the Holy Cross Hospital. Same thing with my brother Randy. Now, they're -- I got -- we've got a sister -- his wife to see him. They never come to see me. You tell me what kind of family I got. Now, you take John and Betty Alvin. I think the world of them. Can you imagine, she took me in, clothed me, washed me, clothes and all. I couldn't clean the house. She got the whole family to come in here and clean my whole house. I couldn't do nothing. I don't know. Sometimes I wish I never -- never existed in this world, but there was a reason. What do you want?

sp.speaker: Manuela Capiak
sp.p: Tell me something about the Army you like.

sp.speaker: Louis Budz
sp.p: What I liked about the Army? You meet a lot of people, you know a lot of people, you know a lot of officers and you get respect from them and I respect them. And I always felt -- a colonel -- I says, "I respect the uniform, Captain." I said, "You are a wonderful person." You know that makes them feel good. They still like me. Like that Captain Street and his wife, I used to fix everything in their house. Then I told them, "Geez, your company commander is my captain. She says, "You are about the nicest person I ever met." I said -- I told her it's my nature.

I don't like people -- I don't hate people. I don't care what color or creed you are. My mother always said, "Never -- don't hate nobody regardless who they are or what they look like." She was right. But my father was right. God gave you brains. Use every bit of it. But I wish he had the brains that I got now. He wouldn't be drunk. I don't know.

There's a reason for God putting me, but what it is, I don't know. I always pray to God. I go to bed and I said, "Dear God, if I should die before I wake, take me soul to keep." And then I say the Our Father, then -- first Act of Contrition, then I say, "Lord, I know I'm not worthy if thou should come, but only say the word and I'll be healed."

Now, you remember when our Lord died on the cross and he looked down on the people. The people are crying for him -- no, he was carrying the cross, that's right -- and the people was crying. He said, "Do not cry for me. Cry for yourself and your children." Do you know what he meant by that? I bet you don't know. Because I'll tell you the truth, but don't be ashamed.

Now, if a boy wants to get married, they -- whoever it is, he's got to have intercourse. You know, that's what you've got to do. That's what it's all about. That's what he's talking about. See, you've got to understand that. See, when I was a little boy I was raped. I wanted to kill that guy, honest. I was a little kid. I didn't know what it -- what it was all about.

But I wasn't in love with none of the girls. They were all too lazy. I think it was about -- let's see. I was going to St. Rosalina. I come out right after I got shot and I didn't know what the hell it meant. Then when I got older in the Army, then I found out what it was all about. Oh, I -- I looked at him and I spotted the old man. I called him, "You son of a" -- oh, I was madder than firecracker. And I called him -- said, "You and your lousy daughter, you can keep her. Let her go to work like I had to go to work." And I said, "Don't you ever come by my mother." Because he lied to my mother. He had a beautiful daughter.

I didn't care to get married. I didn't want to get married. I told my father I didn't want to get married. That's when everything started. I think through me my father was mad. He knew what was going to go happen to me. Boy, was I mad, because he was trying to choke me and everything. Boy, I tell you, he pulled my pants down and I was madder than hell. Boy, I was mad, I tell you one thing.

Now I know what they mean by giving blood to another person so you can be an in-law or your brother-in-law. That's what it's all about. That's what marriage is all -- so you remember that. And if you ever do, make sure you've got a guy that's got a good heart. I wish I had met and married you when I was young, because you've got a good heart. Looking at your eyes and your face, that's all you need. Your smile is pretty. Your eyes are pretty, your ears, nose and all. I tell you. I had a picture. I was 17 years old. I don't know what happened to it. I was in the CCC camps. That's when I started -- I was about 98 -- 90 pounds. I was there for about a couple of years. Jean, when I come over and looked at her, she didn't know who I was. I put on muscles and everything.

Geez, she -- but it was good to go home and eat a Polish meal. See, I had good teeth. Like on that picture, I had all nice teeth. The same thing like now. You know, the VA Hospital fixed them for me. This was a dentist that had 50 years as a dentist and I told him -- he was in the Army and Marines, too. He fixed the first one; they were too big. I had big teeth. I couldn't chew with them. But he fixed these. They fit perfect. They put your Social Security number on there. I don't think you can see it. It's worn out. See, there. [Veteran gives social security number] You know when you get the fire -- make sure you get a suction, but don't put that Fix-a-Dent on them. You don't have to use that. See, I don't put that Fix -- I used to use it on the other teeth. This I don't. They fit good. Oh, well. But the bottoms are good. You can tell how crooked my jaw is. You see where I shot? This side is lower and this side is up higher. You see it's at an angle. Oh, geez.

I'll never forget that bullet going into me. But I know what it means to suffer. When God suffered, carrying that cross, the thorns cutting on his head. And what those soldiers did to him, they were in hell burning. I told him, I said, "Lord" -- I always say, "Lord, I'm not worth if thou should come but let my soul be healed." I say the rosary and I go to bed. And then later I say, "Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me. Lord Jesus Christ have mercy on me." I keep saying it until I get tired, then I fall asleep. God is my judge. Let him judge me how he wants to. But I tell you one -- tell you everything I seen and what I done and all the countries I visited, just think what it would cost me. Thousands and thousands and thousands and thousands of dollars. My life wasn't charmed. It's always work, work, just so we could live and help my -- help my sister out because she couldn't -- she used to make $15 a week. $15 a week. I'd send money home. If I made half a buck, I'd bring it home. Half a dollar would buy a lot of food. You'd be surprised. Now, for five dollars, when Goldblatt's -- it was a different store, but at that time it was Goldblatt's -- for five dollars you'd go in there and get a whole truckload of groceries. Everything was a penny. Penny this, penny that, penny for sugar, butter and all that.

There was open _____+ and Meyers stores and all these other stores. I used to ________+ national _____ and the gangsters hang around there, too. A gangster, when I was doing some work like that Capone, have four -- two, two, two, two, on North Clark Street like that.

And right from there, there was a restaurant used to eat there. He had his house over there. They were killing everybody on St. Valentine's Massacre. I can remember all that stuff. I don't know. But I sure liked the Army. I don't know what's in my blood. I wish I'd never got out. But what are you going to do? They don't want you. Once you get sick, you get sick and you're done. You can't do the things you want to. I couldn't get a steady job. I used to work with a tile setter. I worked for a contractor builder, then he started cheating me out of my pay. I quit him. Then I worked in the guy's garage. They made me change tires. What the hell. I've been -- I knew more about the inside of motors than half the guys did. They're going on the computer and never made it right. I told them, You're wasting time with that." I said, "I'll fix that up in five minutes. It's taken you two hours to do that."

You could tell how hard I worked. See how big my veins are? Look here. Boy, summertime, they get that big. That's when the blood flows. I don't know where I got that burn. The rifle burnt me here. It was so hot. Boom, boom, boom. It fell on me. Oh, geez, I looked. I couldn't -- I was spitting on it to keep it, you know, from burning. I had no Band-Aid, nothing like that. The lieutenant said, "What happened?" I said, "The rifle bounced off my hand after I got through firing it and it got hot on me and that's what happened." Geez, I'll never forget that. They burn -- I couldn't hold the rifle.

You take a clip, you go like this, you pull it back and you go, boop, boop, let it go, boop, goes right in. _______. Boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, don't stop. Put in another clip. The clip stops up, put another one in. Boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. Anyway, you know -- see, I forgot this in the Army. If I think what I did now ______+ was a squad leader. I would have had the guys had their rifles faced like that. Just like this. You know why? If you shoot this way, they can come in between the fire --
[End of Tape One]
